items.title: Session 2: Requirements Definition
items.notes_license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; attribution and noncommercial/share-alike restrictions apply
original_notes: Requirements should state what is expected before detailed design begins, then be refined iteratively as design decisions expose lower-level needs.
Vague or unachievable requirements and missing requirements create downstream cost and schedule risk.
The Mars Climate Orbiter example illustrates that written interface requirements are not enough: units and interface conformance must be verified in implementation.

items.title: Session 9: Verification and Validation
items.notes_license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; attribution and noncommercial/share-alike restrictions apply
original_notes: The lecture explicitly covers design verification and validation, design testing, technical risk management and flight-readiness review.
Use it to distinguish whether an artifact was built according to specification (verification) from whether it satisfies the intended need (validation).

items.title: Lecture 15: Statistical Sins and Wrap Up
items.course: 6.0002 Introduction to Computational Thinking and Data Science (Fall 2016)
items.notes_license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; attribution and noncommercial/share-alike restrictions apply
original_notes: A chart can mislead through inappropriate axis scaling; the correct scale depends on the phenomenon and the question, not a rigid rule that every axis must start at zero.
Short-term fluctuations must not be confused with long-term trends; the analysis window should match the timescale of the phenomenon.
Cherry-picking endpoints or observations can manufacture a desired trend in either direction; inspect the full series and disclose selection choices.
